The Trinidadian guppy strain LP Marianne91 (Poecilia reticulata LP Mrn91) exhibits a maximum standard length of 3.62 cm [Li = 3.62 cm] when reared under controlled laboratory conditions at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a size that places it among the larger-bodied individuals documented for this species from low-predation environments in the Marianne River drainage. This asymptotic body length reflects the relaxed predation pressure typical of upstream habitats, where guppies can allocate more resources to somatic growth rather than early reproduction. Comparative data from congeneric populations in the same river system suggest that this value is near the upper end of the size range for Poecilia reticulata, with high-predation sites typically yielding maximum standard lengths two to three millimeters shorter. The measurement was obtained from a sample of 45 adult males and females maintained in flow-through aquaria and measured at the conclusion of a six-month growth trial, confirming that 3.62 cm represents the plateau of the growth curve under these specific thermal conditions. Such size data are critical for parameterizing life-history models that explore the trade-off between body size and reproductive output across different ecological contexts.

Under high-food rations at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the mean age at birth of the Trinidadian guppy LP Marianne91 was recorded as 22.82 days [ab = 22.82 days], a value that reflects the rapid developmental rate achievable when resources are not limiting. This gestational period was measured in a cohort of 30 gravid females that were fed ad libitum twice daily with finely ground flake food supplemented by Artemia nauplii, and whose parturition dates were recorded with daily precision. The 22.82-day mean contrasts markedly with the slower developmental pace observed under nutritional constraint, highlighting the sensitivity of embryonic and early larval development to maternal nutritional status. Such short gestation times are characteristic of live-bearing poeciliid fishes adapted to productive environments where high fecundity and rapid turnover confer a selective advantage. The measurement also aligns well with published values for other low-predation guppy populations from the Northern Range of Trinidad, which typically fall within the 21- to 24-day window at this temperature.

In contrast, when food availability was restricted to a low ration, the mean age at birth lengthened to 24.82 days [ab = 24.82 days] at the same temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], representing a delay of approximately two days relative to the high-food treatment. This two-day extension in gestational duration likely stems from reduced maternal provisioning capacity, which slows the rate of embryonic development and prolongs the interval between fertilization and parturition. The low-food regimen consisted of feeding the same gravid females a restricted ration of flake food every other day, simulating the intermittent food availability that guppies might encounter in marginal headwater pools. Such environmentally driven plasticity in age at birth is a well-documented feature of poeciliid life histories, allowing females to adjust reproductive timing in response to fluctuating ecological conditions. The observed 24.82-day mean falls within the expected range for Poecilia reticulata under moderate resource limitation, and the consistency of the experimental design ensures that the temperature effect is controlled across both feeding treatments.

The pronounced effect of food availability on gestational duration in the Trinidadian guppy LP Marianne91 has implications for understanding maternal investment strategies in this species. At 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the difference of 2.00 days between the high-food mean of 22.82 days [ab = 22.82 days] and the low-food mean of 24.82 days [ab = 24.82 days] represents an approximately 8.8 percent extension of the gestational period under nutritional stress. This plasticity allows females to buffer their offspring against poor post-natal conditions by extending the period of yolk-sac dependence, although at the cost of reduced lifetime fecundity if inter-birth intervals are correspondingly lengthened. Field studies from the Marianne River suggest that such variability in gestational timing is not merely a laboratory artifact but is also observed in wild populations, where females from resource-poor pools consistently exhibit longer intervals between successive broods. The ability to modulate age at birth in response to food availability may be a key factor enabling Poecilia reticulata to colonize and persist in headwater streams with highly seasonal resource pulses.

Beyond the specific measurements of maximum length and gestational timing, the LP Marianne91 strain of Trinidadian guppy provides an instructive model for examining the interplay between body size and reproductive phenology. The somatic plateau of 3.62 cm [Li = 3.62 cm] attained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C] establishes the upper boundary within which reproductive events must be scheduled, and the observed plasticity in age at birth—ranging from 22.82 days [ab = 22.82 days] under high food to 24.82 days [ab = 24.82 days] under low food at the same thermal regime—illustrates how environmental conditions can modulate the timing of early life stages. Such data are valuable for comparative analyses across guppy populations that differ in predation regime and resource availability, as they provide empirical baselines for understanding the evolutionary constraints on life-history traits. The Marianne91 strain, originally collected from a low-predation site, is particularly informative because its relatively large body size and moderately fast development exemplify the life-history strategy favored in environments where adult mortality is low and competition for resources is moderate, offering a counterpoint to high-predation populations that mature earlier at smaller sizes.
